blogs.title: Multi-tenant GPU Kubernetes on simulated hardware with Kamaji and HAMi
blogs.content: Posted on October 23, 2026 by By Anish Bista | CNCF Golden Kubestronaut CNCF projects highlighted in this post GPU teams usually face a bad trade-off. Give every team its own Kubernetes cluster and you pay for a control plane per team. Put everyone in one shared cluster and you get weak isolation. Either way, Kubernetes hands out GPUs as whole cards, so a pod that needs 4 GB of an 80 GB GPU still blocks the entire card. This post shows a way out by combining two open-source projects: Kamaji runs each tenant’s Kubernetes control plane as pods inside one management cluster. HAMi lets pods request a slice of a GPU (memory in MB, compute in %) and packs several pods onto one card. I built the whole thing on a single machine with no physical GPU, using HAMi’s mock device plugin to simulate the cards. The result: two fully isolated tenant clusters, each scheduling fractional-GPU workloads through HAMi, with all eight tests passing. Everything below is reproducible: the exact versions, the commands that worked, the errors I hit and how I fixed them. Architecture One kind cluster hosts Kamaji and both tenant control planes; each tenant’s worker is a separate container that joins over the kind network and runs HAMi. Tenants never share a node or an API server. The only shared pieces are the management cluster and the kamaji-etcd datastore, where each tenant’s data is kept separate. Why Kamaji + HAMi Kamaji solves the cluster problem and HAMi solves the GPU problem; they work at different layers, so they don’t overlap. The interesting part is where they meet. A tenant’s API server lives in the management cluster, but HAMi’s webhook lives on the tenant’s worker nodes. Every GPU pod creation therefore depends on the API server reaching back into the tenant through Kamaji’s Konnectivity tunnel. Proving that path works was the main goal of this lab. Lab setup Everything runs as Docker containers on one Linux host; 4 CPU cores, 8 GB of free RAM and 20 GB of disk are enough. How do you test GPU sharing without a GPU? HAMi’s real device plugin talks to the NVIDIA driver, so it can’t start without hardware. The mock device plugin skips hardware discovery. You describe fake cards in a node annotation, and it registers gpumem and gpucores capacity from that. HAMi’s webhook, scheduler and quota logic then run exactly as they would on real nodes. Two simulated setups make the tenants easy to tell apart: tenant-a: 1 × NVIDIA A100 80 GB (81,920 MB, 100 cores) tenant-b: 2 × NVIDIA L4 24 GB (49,152 MB, 200 cores) Step-by-step build The build has five steps; step 3 creates both tenants at once, and steps 4 and 5 are repeated per tenant. Plain kubectl talks to the management cluster; --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig talks to a tenant. Step 1: Management cluster, cert-manager and MetalLB kind create cluster --name kamaji kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.21.2/cert-manager.yaml kubectl -n cert-manager wait pod --all --for=condition=Ready --timeout=180s kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/v0.16.1/config/manifests/metallb-frr-k8s.yaml kubectl -n metallb-system wait pod --all --for=condition=Ready --timeout=180s Find your kind network’s IPv4 subnet, then give MetalLB a range at the top of it: docker network inspect kind | grep Subnet cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1 kind: IPAddressPool metadata: name: kind-ip-pool namespace: metallb-system spec: addresses: - 172.18.255.200-172.18.255.250 --- apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1 kind: L2Advertisement metadata: name: empty namespace: metallb-system EOF Step 2: Install Kamaji helm repo add clastix https://clastix.github.io/charts helm upgrade --install kamaji clastix/kamaji \ --namespace kamaji-system --create-namespace \ --set 'resources=null' --version 0.0.0+latest kubectl -n kamaji-system get pods Step 3: Create the Tenant Control Planes This creates both tenants, tenant-a and tenant-b : export TENANT_VERSION=v1.36.4 kubectl create namespace tenants for t in tenant-a tenant-b; do cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: kamaji.clastix.io/v1alpha1 kind: TenantControlPlane metadata: name: ${t} namespace: tenants labels: tenant.clastix.io: ${t} spec: controlPlane: deployment: replicas: 1 service: serviceType: LoadBalancer kubernetes: version: "${TENANT_VERSION}" kubelet: configurationJSONPatches: - op: add path: /cgroupDriver value: systemd networkProfile: port: 6443 podCidr: 10.244.0.0/16 addons: coreDNS: {} kubeProxy: {} konnectivity: server: port: 8132 agent: mode: DaemonSet EOF done Once both tenant control plane pods are Running, save a kubeconfig for each tenant: for t in tenant-a tenant-b; do kubectl -n tenants get secret ${t}-admin-kubeconfig -o jsonpath='{.data.admin\.conf}' | base64 -d > ${t}.kubeconfig kubectl --kubeconfig ${t}.kubeconfig cluster-info Done Each tenant control plane is a single pod in the tenants namespace of the management cluster, running on the kamaji-control-plane node. The 4/4 in the READY column are its four containers: kube-apiserver : the tenant’s API server, exposed through the MetalLB IP kube-scheduler : the tenant’s default scheduler kube-controller-manager : runs the tenant’s built-in controllers konnectivity-server : the management-cluster end of the tunnel that lets the API server reach the tenant’s worker nodes Step 4: Join a worker node Kamaji has no kind helper for workers, so the worker is a kindest/node container on the kind network, joined with standard kubeadm. Its version must match the tenant. docker run -d --name tenant-a-worker --hostname tenant-a-worker \ --network kind --privileged \ --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined \ --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run -v /var -v /lib/modules:/lib/modules:ro \ kindest/node:v1.36.4@sha256:099e049362a1526b2db71494e1947aae99bd16290d7c895f2b7ea312e3cbfaed sleep 15 docker exec -i tenant-a-worker sh -c 'cat > /root/tenant-a.kubeconfig' < tenant-a.kubeconfig JOIN_CMD=$(docker exec tenant-a-worker kubeadm token create --print-join-command \ --kubeconfig /root/tenant-a.kubeconfig) echo "$JOIN_CMD" docker exec tenant-a-worker bash -c "${JOIN_CMD} --ignore-preflight-errors=all" Install Calico in the tenant (not the management cluster), with its pool set to the tenant podCidr : curl -sLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.31.2/manifests/calico.yaml sed -i 's|# - name: CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR|- name: CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR|; s|# value: "192.168.0.0/16"| value: "10.244.0.0/16"|' calico.yaml kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig apply -f calico.yaml kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig get nodes Step 5: HAMi and mock GPUs in the tenant # Don’t label the worker gpu=on; that starts HAMi’s real NVIDIA device plugin, which fails without a driver. export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/tenant-a.kubeconfig helm repo add hami-charts https://project-hami.github.io/HAMi/ helm install hami hami-charts/hami -n kube-system # wait for hami-scheduler Running, and the hami-scheduler-device ConfigMap to exist kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Project-HAMi/mock-device-plugin/master/k8s-mock-rbac.yaml kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Project-HAMi/mock-device-plugin/master/k8s-mock-plugin.yaml # Simulate 1 x A100 80 GB NODE=tenant-a-worker kubectl patch node $NODE --subresource=status --type=json \ -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/status/capacity/nvidia.com~1gpu","value":"10"}]' kubectl annotate node $NODE \ 'hami.io/node-nvidia-register=[{"id":"GPU-MOCK-0","count":10,"devmem":81920,"devcore":100,"type":"NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB","health":true,"numa":0,"mode":"hami-core"}]' About 30 seconds later the node advertises the fake card: { "nvidia.com/gpu": "10", "nvidia.com/gpucores": "100", "nvidia.com/gpumem": "81920", "nvidia.com/gpumem-percentage": "100" } For tenant-b , repeat steps 4 and 5 with tenant-b names.
